position: attributive only — before a noun (*the reported cases*); after a verb it is the passive verb, not the adjective

senses.gloss: Said by the news or by officials to be true, though not proved.
examples: The *reported* number of cases keeps going up.
The *reported* cause of the fire was a space heater.
*Reported* crime is down, but that isn't the same as crime being down.

senses.gloss: So wrong that it deserves strong criticism.
examples: His behavior at the meeting was *reprehensible*.
Lying to the families was a *reprehensible* thing to do.
Nothing is more *reprehensible* than blaming the victim.

senses.gloss: In art, showing people and things as they really look.
examples: He likes *representational* art better than abstract painting.
Her early work was strictly *representational*.
The museum has a whole floor of *representational* painting.

contrast: Also a common noun: *a sales representative*, *our representative in Congress*.

senses.gloss: Typical of a larger group, so that it shows what the whole group is like.
examples: The sample was not *representative* of the country as a whole.
Is this painting *representative* of his later work?
We need a more *representative* group of testers.

senses.gloss: Working through elected officials who act for the people.
examples: The United States has a *representative* democracy.
*Representative* government was the whole point of the revolution.

senses.gloss: Pushed down and never expressed, of a feeling or a memory.
examples: Years of *repressed* anger came out at once.
He talked about his *repressed* memories of the accident.

senses.gloss: Unable to show feelings or enjoy things, of a person.
examples: She describes her family as cold and *repressed*.
He was the most *repressed* person I have ever worked with.

senses.gloss: Using force and strict control to keep people from being free.
examples: They fled a *repressive* regime.
The new law is the most *repressive* in decades.
The government grew more *repressive* after the protests.

senses.gloss: Able to be done again by someone else with the same result.
examples: The results have to be *reproducible* by other labs.
Their findings turned out not to be *reproducible*.
Science depends on *reproducible* experiments.

senses.gloss: Having to do with producing babies or young.
examples: The clinic focuses on *reproductive* health.
*Reproductive* rights were on the ballot this year.
Salmon return to the river in the *reproductive* season.

senses.gloss: Belonging to, or looking like, snakes, lizards and other reptiles.
examples: The museum has a whole *reptilian* collection.
Its skin is dry and *reptilian* to the touch.

senses.gloss: Cold and unpleasant, in the way a snake seems to people.
examples: His smile was *more reptilian* than friendly.
She played the lawyer with a *reptilian* calm.

ru: республиканский (о партии США); республиканский (о форме правления)
comparison: not gradable — but *very Republican* when it means 'typical of the party'
contrast: Capital *Republican* is the American political party; small-letter *republican* is about a republic as a form of government. Capitalized, it is also a noun: *She's a Republican*.

senses.gloss: Belonging to or supporting the Republican Party of the United States.
examples: She comes from a *Republican* family in Texas.
The state has been solidly *Republican* for decades.

senses.gloss: Having to do with a republic, a country run by elected leaders and not a king.
examples: France has a long *republican* tradition.
They fought for a *republican* form of government.

senses.gloss: So wrong or unpleasant that it disgusts you.
examples: The very idea was *repugnant* to her.
He called the comments morally *repugnant*.
Nothing is more *repugnant* to most Americans than censorship.

senses.gloss: Extremely unpleasant to look at, smell or think about.
examples: The smell in the fridge was *repulsive*.
I find his politics *repulsive*.
She plays a *repulsive* villain who somehow makes you laugh.

contrast: The stress is on the first syllable, REP-yuh-tuh-buhl, even though *reputation* stresses the third.

senses.gloss: Known to be honest and to do good work.
examples: Buy the part from a *reputable* dealer.
The story came from a *reputable* source.
Theirs is the most *reputable* firm in the city.

senses.gloss: That you must do or have, because a rule says so.
examples: *Required* courses take up most of the first year.
A signature is *required* on both forms.
All visitors are *required* to sign in at the desk.

contrast: Formal. Everyday English says *required* or *necessary*. Do not confuse it with the noun *prerequisite*, the course or condition you need first.

senses.gloss: Needed for a particular purpose.
examples: She has the *requisite* experience for the job.
He filled out the *requisite* forms and waited.
The team lacks the *requisite* funding.

senses.gloss: Angry and bitter because you feel you have been treated unfairly.
examples: He was *resentful* of his brother's success.
She grew *resentful* about doing all the housework.
Years later he is still *resentful* that nobody thanked him.

senses.gloss: Not saying much about your feelings; quiet with people you don't know.
examples: Her father is a *reserved* man who rarely says much.
He seems cold at first, but he is just *reserved*.

senses.gloss: Kept for one particular person or purpose.
examples: This table is *reserved*.
The front row is *reserved* for family.

position: attributive only — mostly; formal writing also puts it after the noun: *a citizen resident abroad*
contrast: Much more common as a noun: *local residents*, *a hospital resident* (a young doctor in training).

senses.gloss: Living in a place, especially permanently.
examples: The *resident* population doubles every summer.
Students *resident* in the state pay less tuition.

senses.gloss: Working at one place all the time instead of visiting.
examples: She is our *resident* expert on tax law.
The hotel has a *resident* chef and a *resident* cat.

senses.gloss: Made up of homes rather than stores, offices or factories.
examples: They live in a quiet *residential* neighborhood.
The whole block is *residential*, so there are no shops.
*Residential* streets have a 25 mile-an-hour limit.

senses.gloss: Where you live on site while you take part in a program.
examples: He spent six weeks in a *residential* treatment program.
The college has a *residential* requirement for freshmen.

contrast: In film and television *residuals* is a noun: the payments an actor gets each time a show is aired again.

senses.gloss: Left over after most of something is gone.
examples: There is still some *residual* pain in the knee.
*Residual* chemicals stayed in the soil for years.
He has a *residual* fear of big dogs.

senses.gloss: Able to recover quickly after trouble or illness.
examples: Kids are more *resilient* than we give them credit for.
The local economy proved surprisingly *resilient*.

senses.gloss: Springing back into shape after being bent or pressed.
examples: The foam is light and *resilient*.
Pick a *resilient* flooring for the kitchen.

form: also the second half of compounds: *heat-resistant*, *water-resistant*

senses.gloss: Not harmed or affected by something.
examples: These bacteria are *resistant* to most antibiotics.
Choose a stain-*resistant* fabric for the couch.

senses.gloss: Unwilling to accept something and quietly fighting it.
examples: Older staff were *resistant* to the change.
He is *resistant* to any kind of therapy.

senses.gloss: Firm about what you have decided, and not changing your mind.
examples: She was *resolute* in her decision to leave.
The mayor stayed *resolute* under a week of pressure.
He gave a *resolute* answer: no.

takes: *with* + noun; *for* or *with* + person, in the 'meaningful' sense

senses.gloss: Deep, clear and continuing, of a sound or a voice.
examples: He has a deep, *resonant* voice.
The old bell gave a *resonant* hum.

senses.gloss: Full of a meaning that stays with people.
examples: The film is *resonant* with memories of childhood.
Her speech was especially *resonant* for young voters.

senses.gloss: Complete and unmistakable, of a success, a defeat or an answer.
examples: The show was a *resounding* success.
The proposal met with a *resounding* no.

senses.gloss: Loud and echoing.
examples: There was a *resounding* crash from the kitchen.
The speech got a *resounding* cheer.

senses.gloss: Good at finding a way to solve problems with whatever you have.
examples: She is the most *resourceful* person on the team.
*Resourceful* cooks can make dinner out of almost nothing.
You have to be *resourceful* when the budget is this small.

contrast: Three words that learners mix up: *respected* — admired by other people; *respectful* — behaving politely toward someone; *respective* — belonging to each one separately.

senses.gloss: Admired by other people because of what you do or know.
examples: He is a widely *respected* surgeon.
The paper is *respected* on both sides of the aisle.
She is one of the most *respected* judges in the state.

contrast: Not *respectful* (polite) and not *respected* (admired). *Respective* always goes with a plural noun and means 'each one's own'.

senses.gloss: Belonging to each of the people or things just named, separately.
examples: After the meeting they went back to their *respective* offices.
The two companies kept their *respective* names.
Each writer spoke about their *respective* field.

senses.gloss: Having to do with breathing and the lungs.
examples: He was treated for a *respiratory* infection.
Smoke can cause serious *respiratory* problems.
The virus attacks the *respiratory* system.

position: both — most often after a verb or right after the noun: *the general, resplendent in blue*
contrast: Literary. You meet it in writing and in wedding announcements, not in everyday speech.

senses.gloss: Looking splendid, bright and colorful.
examples: She arrived *resplendent* in a red silk gown.
The hall was *resplendent* with flowers.
The general stood on the steps, *resplendent* in full uniform.

senses.gloss: Reacting quickly and well to what people need or say.
examples: The staff was friendly and *responsive*.
The mayor has to be more *responsive* to voters.

senses.gloss: Reacting well to treatment or to a control.
examples: The tumor was *responsive* to the new drug.
The steering is light and *responsive*.

position: predicative only — before a noun only in the compound *well-rested*: *a well-rested team*

senses.gloss: Feeling fresh again because you have slept or relaxed.
examples: I felt *rested* for the first time in weeks.
You'll play better *rested*.
A short nap left her *rested* and ready to work.

contrast: *Restful* describes the thing that gives you rest; *rested* describes the person who got it. *A restful weekend leaves you rested.*

senses.gloss: Calm and quiet, so that it helps you relax.
examples: We had a *restful* weekend at the lake.
The room is painted a *restful* green.
Nothing is more *restful* than a quiet morning.

contrast: Close to *restless*, but *restive* adds impatience with being held back or controlled: a *restive* crowd is about to stop obeying.

senses.gloss: Unwilling to keep waiting or to be controlled, and beginning to show it.
examples: The crowd grew *restive* as the delay went on.
*Restive* lawmakers began to question the plan.
The horses were *restive* before the storm.

senses.gloss: Unable to stay still or be patient, because you are bored or worried.
examples: The kids get *restless* on long drives.
He was *restless* all evening before the interview.

senses.gloss: Broken and without real rest, of a night or of sleep.
examples: She had a *restless* night.
It was a *restless* sleep full of strange dreams.

senses.gloss: Making you feel strong and fresh again.
examples: A hot bath is wonderfully *restorative*.
She took a *restorative* week off in the mountains.

senses.gloss: Aimed at repairing harm rather than punishing.
examples: The school uses *restorative* justice instead of suspensions.
He does *restorative* dental work.

senses.gloss: Calm and controlled; not extreme or showy.
examples: His reaction was surprisingly *restrained*.
The design is elegant and *restrained*.
She gave a *restrained* smile and said nothing.

senses.gloss: Controlled, so that only certain people may enter or use it.
examples: This is a *restricted* area — you need a badge.
The documents are *restricted*.

senses.gloss: Limited in amount, range or choice.
examples: He is on a *restricted* diet after the surgery.
The team works with a very *restricted* budget.

senses.gloss: Limiting what people can do, usually more than they think is fair.
examples: The dress code is too *restrictive*.
These are the most *restrictive* voting laws in the state's history.
*Restrictive* rules drove the best players away.

senses.gloss: Becoming strong, popular or common again after a weak period.
examples: A *resurgent* auto industry brought jobs back to the city.
The team faces a *resurgent* rival on Sunday.
Measles is *resurgent* in states with low vaccination rates.

senses.gloss: Done to punish someone for something they did to you first.
examples: The country launched a *retaliatory* strike.
He says the firing was *retaliatory*.
*Retaliatory* tariffs hit farmers hardest.

contrast: *Reticent* is about not speaking; *reluctant* is about not wanting to act. You are *reticent* about your past but *reluctant* to leave.

senses.gloss: Not willing to talk about something or to say what you think.
examples: He is *reticent* about his years in the army.
She was oddly *reticent* during the whole meeting.
Witnesses were more *reticent* than the police had expected.

senses.gloss: No longer working, because you have reached the end of your working life.
examples: My neighbor is a *retired* teacher.
Both of my parents are *retired* now.
He is a *retired* Navy officer who still gets up at five.

position: both — the 'leaving office' sense only before a noun

senses.gloss: Shy, and staying out of the center of attention.
examples: He is a *retiring* man who hates parties.
She is shy and *retiring* in a big group.

senses.gloss: About to leave a job or an office for good.
senses.ru: уходящий в отставку, уходящий на пенсию
examples: The *retiring* chairman gave a short speech.
They threw a party for the *retiring* principal.

senses.gloss: Able to be pulled back in or folded away.
examples: The stadium has a *retractable* roof.
Cats have *retractable* claws.
The blade is *retractable*, which makes it safer to carry.

senses.gloss: Copying the style of an earlier time on purpose, usually the 1950s to the 1980s.
examples: The diner has a *retro* look, right down to the jukebox.
Her whole outfit is very *retro*.
*Retro* video games are selling again.

senses.gloss: Taking effect from a date in the past, not only from today.
examples: The raise is *retroactive* to January 1.
Congress passed a *retroactive* tax change.
The new rule is not *retroactive*, so old cases stand.

contrast: Also a noun: *a retrospective* is a show of an artist's work from across their whole career.

senses.gloss: Looking back at things that happened or were made in the past.
examples: The study is *retrospective*, based on old medical records.
He took a *retrospective* look at thirty years on the job.
The team holds a *retrospective* meeting after every project.

senses.gloss: Coming back after being away, or taking part again after a break.
examples: *Returning* students register on Monday.
The *returning* champion took the court first.
*Returning* soldiers were met at the airport by their families.

senses.gloss: Able to be used again instead of thrown away.
examples: Bring a *reusable* bag to the store.
The containers are *reusable* and dishwasher safe.
We switched to *reusable* water bottles last year.

senses.gloss: Showing a lot of the body, of clothes.
examples: The dress was a little too *revealing* for the office.
She wore something less *revealing* to the interview.

senses.gloss: Telling you something important that was not obvious before.
examples: His answer was very *revealing*.
It is the most *revealing* interview she has ever given.

senses.gloss: Deeply respected, almost in the way holy things are respected.
examples: He is *revered* as the father of the sport.
She is a *revered* figure in American poetry.
The old cookbook is *revered* by chefs.

senses.gloss: Showing deep respect, the way people behave in a holy place.
examples: The crowd fell into a *reverent* silence.
He speaks about his old teacher in *reverent* tones.
The movie takes a *reverent* approach to its subject.

contrast: Also a noun (*the reverse is true*) and a verb (*reverse the car*). As an adjective it goes only before a noun — for 'the opposite' after a verb, say *the opposite*.

senses.gloss: Opposite in direction or order to the usual one.
examples: Put the names in *reverse* order.
The truck has a *reverse* camera.
Critics called the policy *reverse* discrimination.

senses.gloss: Able to be changed back to the way it was.
examples: The damage is *reversible* if you stop now.
Most of these side effects are *reversible*.

senses.gloss: Able to be worn with either side outward.
examples: It is a *reversible* jacket — black on one side, red on the other.
*Reversible* belts save you buying two.

contrast: In American English *revise* means to change a text or a figure. It does not mean 'study for an exam' — that British use is *review* or *study* here.

senses.gloss: Changed and corrected from an earlier version.
examples: Use the *revised* edition, not the old one.
The *revised* figures are much lower.
Here is the *revised* schedule for next week.

contrast: In this everyday sense it has nothing to do with *revolt* 'to rebel', so *the revolting peasants* is an old English joke.

senses.gloss: So unpleasant that it almost makes you feel sick.
examples: The smell in the basement was *revolting*.
He told a *revolting* joke at dinner.
That is the most *revolting* thing I have ever tasted.

contrast: Also a noun: *a revolutionary* is a person who fights to overthrow a government.

senses.gloss: Completely new and changing the way things are done.
examples: The first iPhone was a *revolutionary* design.
Her way of teaching reading was *revolutionary* at the time.

senses.gloss: Having to do with a political revolution.
examples: *Revolutionary* leaders took over the capital within a week.
The group had openly *revolutionary* aims.

contrast: It is about satisfaction, not money: a job can be *rewarding* and still badly paid. For money say *well-paid*.

senses.gloss: Giving you the good feeling that the effort was worth it.
examples: Teaching is hard work, but it is *rewarding*.
It was the most *rewarding* year of my life.
Small children are exhausting and *rewarding* to raise.

senses.gloss: Asked for effect, not because you want an answer — of a question.
examples: Don't answer — it was a *rhetorical* question.
He ended with a *rhetorical* question about fairness.

senses.gloss: Having to do with the art of speaking and writing persuasively.
examples: It is a *rhetorical* device, not a real promise.
Her *rhetorical* skill won the debate.

contrast: In practice you meet it in one phrase, *rheumatoid arthritis*. The silent *rh-* is simply 'r'.

senses.gloss: Of the disease in which the body attacks its own joints and they swell and hurt.
examples: She was diagnosed with *rheumatoid* arthritis at thirty.
*Rheumatoid* arthritis is an autoimmune disease.
He takes a weekly shot for his *rheumatoid* arthritis.

senses.gloss: Ending in the same sound as another word or another line.
examples: The poem is written in *rhyming* couplets.
Little kids love *rhyming* books.
'Cat' and 'hat' are a *rhyming* pair.

senses.gloss: Having a regular, repeated beat or movement.
examples: The *rhythmic* sound of the waves put me to sleep.
Her breathing was slow and *rhythmic*.
It is a *rhythmic*, danceable song.

senses.gloss: Old, weak and likely to break or fall over.
examples: We climbed a *rickety* wooden staircase.
The table is *rickety*, so don't lean on it.
They crossed on a *rickety* little bridge.

position: predicative only — after a verb, or right after the noun: *a report riddled with errors*

senses.gloss: Full of holes, especially holes made by bullets.
examples: The road sign was *riddled* with bullet holes.
They found the old boat *riddled* with worm holes.

senses.gloss: Full of something bad, all the way through.
examples: The report was *riddled* with errors.
The whole system is *riddled* with corruption.

contrast: *Ridiculous* means laughably bad or unreasonable. For something meant to make you laugh, say *funny*.

senses.gloss: So silly or unreasonable that nobody can take it seriously.
examples: Twenty dollars for a cup of coffee is *ridiculous*.
He looked *ridiculous* in that hat.
This is the most *ridiculous* rule in the whole handbook.

position: predicative only — never before a noun
contrast: *Rife* is used only about bad things — rumors, corruption, mistakes — and never goes before a noun.

senses.gloss: Very common and everywhere, of something bad; with *with*, full of it.
examples: Rumors were *rife* in the days before the vote.
Corruption is *rife* in the construction business.
The essay is *rife* with spelling mistakes.

senses.gloss: Dishonestly arranged in advance so that a particular side wins.
examples: He claimed the election was *rigged*.
It is a *rigged* game — the house always wins.
The whole contest looked *rigged* from the start.

ru: правый, находящийся справа; правая рука (о человеке)
contrast: *Right-hand* is about position; *right-handed* is about the hand a person writes with.

senses.gloss: On or toward the right side.
examples: Take the *right-hand* lane at the light.
The switch is on the *right-hand* side of the door.

senses.gloss: In *right-hand man* and *right-hand woman*: the person you rely on most.
examples: She is the governor's *right-hand* woman.
He was the boss's *right-hand* man for twenty years.

contrast: Nothing to do with the political right — that is *right-wing*.

senses.gloss: Having the opinions and values the speaker thinks are decent and correct.
examples: No *right-minded* person would defend that.
*Right-minded* citizens spoke up at the meeting.
Every *right-minded* voter should be worried by this.

senses.gloss: Belonging to the conservative side in politics.
examples: He writes for a *right-wing* website.
Her views are pretty *right-wing* for this town.
A *right-wing* group organized the rally.

contrast: The insult is *self-righteous*: certain of being right and showing it.

senses.gloss: Morally right and good, often with a religious feeling to it.
examples: He saw himself as a *righteous* man.
The sermon was about *righteous* living.

senses.gloss: Of anger: felt to be completely justified.
examples: There was *righteous* anger in her voice.
*Righteous* indignation filled the letters page for a week.

senses.gloss: Having the legal or moral right to something — of an owner, an heir or a place.
examples: The painting was returned to its *rightful* owner.
She took her *rightful* place at the top of the rankings.
He is the *rightful* heir to the property.

senses.gloss: Stiff and not bending.
examples: The case has a *rigid* plastic shell.
Keep your arm *rigid* while I wrap it.

senses.gloss: Very strict and not open to change.
examples: The school has *rigid* rules about phones.
He is too *rigid* to work well on a team.

senses.gloss: Careful, thorough and exact.
examples: The drug went through *rigorous* testing.
She is a *rigorous* thinker who checks every number.

senses.gloss: Demanding and hard to keep up with, of a course or a schedule.
examples: It is a *rigorous* program — expect long hours.
They follow a *rigorous* training schedule all winter.

contrast: Informal and cheerful. It goes with *success*, *time* and *adventure*, not with people.

senses.gloss: Full of noisy energy, or very great — of a good time or a success.
examples: They had a *rip-roaring* good time at the fair.
The show was a *rip-roaring* success.
It is a *rip-roaring* adventure movie with no quiet moments.

senses.gloss: Fully grown and ready to eat, of fruit, vegetables or cheese.
examples: The peaches are finally *ripe*.
Pick the *ripest* tomato on the vine.

senses.gloss: Ready for something to happen.
examples: The market is *ripe* for change.
Conditions were *ripe* for a strike.

contrast: In American schools a *rising* senior is a student who will be a senior next fall.

senses.gloss: Going up in amount, level or price.
examples: *Rising* prices are hurting families on a fixed income.
We watched the *rising* water from the porch.

senses.gloss: Becoming more successful or important.
examples: She is a *rising* star in country music.
He is a *rising* senior at the high school.

senses.gloss: Carrying no chance of loss or harm.
examples: There is no such thing as a *risk-free* investment.
The trial is *risk-free* — you can cancel any time.
No surgery is completely *risk-free*.

contrast: *Risky* and *risqué* look alike but are different words: *risky* is about danger, *risqué* is about being slightly indecent.

senses.gloss: Carrying a real chance that something will go wrong.
examples: Driving in that storm was *risky*.
Stocks are *riskier* than bonds.
It is a *risky* plan, but it might work.

form: from French; often written without the accent, *risque*, and the ending is said 'kay'
contrast: Not the same word as *risky*. A *risqué* joke has nothing to do with danger.

senses.gloss: Slightly rude or sexual, in a way that may shock some people.
examples: He told a *risqué* joke at the wedding.
The costumes were a little *risqué* for a family show.
Her act is the most *risqué* on the whole tour.

contrast: Far more common as a noun (*a morning ritual*). The adjective goes only before a noun; after a verb use *ritualistic*.

senses.gloss: Done as part of a ceremony, or always done in the same fixed way.
examples: *Ritual* washing comes before the meal.
The dance had a *ritual* meaning for the village.
There was the *ritual* exchange of gifts at the door.

senses.gloss: Done in a fixed, repeated way, like a ceremony.
examples: The team has a *ritualistic* warm-up before every game.
His hand-washing had become *ritualistic*.
There is something *ritualistic* about Sunday dinner at their house.

contrast: Informal and a little dated. *Fancy* or *upscale* is what people say now.

senses.gloss: Expensive and fashionable.
examples: They stayed at a *ritzy* hotel downtown.
It is the *ritziest* neighborhood in the city.
The place is too *ritzy* for jeans.

form: -ing from *rivet* 'to fasten with a metal pin'

senses.gloss: So interesting that you cannot look away.
examples: The trial made for *riveting* television.
Her testimony was absolutely *riveting*.
It is a *riveting* account of the escape.

senses.gloss: Making a loud, deep, continuous sound.
examples: We sat by a *roaring* fire.
A *roaring* crowd greeted the team at the airport.

senses.gloss: Very great or lively — in a few fixed phrases.
examples: The bake sale was a *roaring* success.
The 1920s are still called the *Roaring* Twenties.

contrast: Before a noun, dish names keep the old form: *roast beef*, *roast chicken*, *roast potatoes*. Everywhere else say *roasted*: *The potatoes were roasted, not fried*.

senses.gloss: Cooked in an oven or over a fire — in the names of dishes.
examples: We had *roast* beef and potatoes.
She ordered the *roast* chicken.
*Roast* duck is the house specialty.

contrast: The everyday form. Only the old dish names use plain *roast* (*roast beef*).

senses.gloss: Cooked or browned with dry heat, in an oven or over a fire.
examples: *Roasted* vegetables are the easiest side dish there is.
The peppers were *roasted* and then peeled.
Try the salad with *roasted* almonds.

senses.gloss: Belonging to or done by robots.
examples: The factory uses a *robotic* arm for welding.
He had *robotic* surgery on his knee.

senses.gloss: Stiff and without feeling, like a machine.
examples: Her voice on the phone was flat and *robotic*.
He gave a *robotic* answer and moved on to the next caller.

senses.gloss: Strong and healthy.
examples: He is eighty and still *robust*.
These plants are *robust* enough to survive a frost.

senses.gloss: Strong and working well, of a system, an economy or a debate.
examples: We need a more *robust* password policy.
Sales were *robust* over the holidays.

senses.gloss: Strong and full, of a taste or smell.
examples: It is a *robust* red wine that stands up to steak.
He likes his coffee dark and *robust*.

contrast: As two words it is a noun phrase: *He hit rock bottom last year*.

senses.gloss: As low as it can possibly go — almost always of prices.
examples: They are selling tickets at *rock-bottom* prices.
Gas hit *rock-bottom* rates that winter.
We got a *rock-bottom* deal on the car.

senses.gloss: Covered with rocks, or made of rock.
examples: They hiked along a *rocky* beach.
The trail gets *rockier* near the top.

senses.gloss: Full of problems and not at all steady.
examples: The marriage got off to a *rocky* start.
It has been a *rocky* year for the company.

senses.gloss: Rising and falling in long gentle slopes, of land.
examples: We drove past *rolling* hills and old farms.
The house sits on forty acres of *rolling* farmland.

senses.gloss: Happening in stages, one area or group at a time.
examples: The city had *rolling* blackouts all August.
They announced a *rolling* schedule of layoffs.

contrast: Also a noun for a person (*the Romans*). With a small letter, *roman* is the plain upright type you are reading now, as opposed to *italic*.

senses.gloss: Of ancient Rome, or of the city of Rome today.
examples: They found a *Roman* coin in the field.
*Roman* roads still run across parts of Europe.
The chapters are numbered with *Roman* numerals.

contrast: Also a noun (*He's a Roman Catholic*). In everyday speech people usually just say *Catholic*.

senses.gloss: Belonging to the Christian church that has the Pope at its head.
examples: She was raised *Roman Catholic*.
They were married in a *Roman Catholic* church.
The hospital is *Roman Catholic* and was founded by nuns.

contrast: A different word from the noun *romance* 'a love story', and it is always capitalized.

senses.gloss: Of the languages that grew out of Latin — French, Spanish, Italian, Portuguese and Romanian.
examples: Spanish and Italian are *Romance* languages.
She studies *Romance* philology.
The *Romance* languages all give nouns a gender.

contrast: Also a noun: the people (*a Romanian*) and the language (*She speaks Romanian*).

senses.gloss: From Romania, or connected with Romania and its language.
examples: He is a *Romanian* filmmaker living in Berlin.
We had dinner at a *Romanian* restaurant.
Her grandparents are *Romanian*.

contrast: Also a noun (*a hopeless romantic*). Capital *Romantic* means the poets and composers of the early 1800s.

senses.gloss: Having to do with love between people.
examples: They are in a *romantic* relationship.
He planned a *romantic* dinner for their anniversary.

senses.gloss: Beautiful in a way that makes you think of love.
examples: Venice at night is impossibly *romantic*.
It is the most *romantic* restaurant in town.

senses.gloss: Idealistic, and not based on how things really are.
examples: He has a *romantic* view of the old West.
That is a *romantic* notion of what soldiers actually do.

senses.gloss: Having plenty of space inside.
examples: The car is surprisingly *roomy* in back.
Their new place is *roomier* than the old one.
I want a *roomy* bag for the trip.

ru: укоренённый, уходящий корнями; приросший к месту
position: both — before a noun with an adverb: *a deeply rooted belief*
comparison: not gradable — the adverb carries the degree: *deeply rooted*, *firmly rooted*
contrast: *Rooted for* is a different verb: to *root for* a team means to cheer for it.

senses.gloss: Coming from something and firmly fixed in it.
examples: The custom is *rooted* in the nineteenth century.
His fear of water is *rooted* in one bad afternoon.

senses.gloss: Unable to move, as if fixed to the ground.
examples: I stood *rooted* to the spot.
She was *rooted* in place by the noise.
